item.title: Egypt Asks for Return of Ancient Mummy Behind Scots Controversy
item.description: Egypt said it has requested the return of the 4,000-year-old mummified remains of a priest whose removal from display at a Glasgow museum due to ethical concerns sparked debate in Scotland.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- Egypt said it has requested the return of the 4,000-year-old mummified remains of a priest whose removal from display at a Glasgow museum due to ethical concerns sparked debate in Scotland.Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum in Scotland’s largest city took the corpse of Nekht out of public view in late October because of a lack of “consent from the deceased” or their descendants, according to local media reports.“We are currently in the process of communicating and taking the measures” required for Nekht’s possible return, Egyptian Tourism Minister Sherif Fathy told Bloomberg by phone. “We shall see how things unfold as such issues aren’t straightforward.”Egypt, where Pharonic-era pyramids, temples and tombs are a major draw for foreign tourists, has long sought the legal return of ancient artifacts that were taken abroad in recent centuries. The North African nation inaugurated the high-tech $1 billion Grand Egyptian Museum last year, which now houses some of its most famed treasures.The Kelvingrove museum’s operators, Glasgow Life, earlier said they’d received an Egyptian request to return Nekht’s remains, without specifying who’d made it.The charity’s decision to remove the mummy from display in Scotland followed a recent change in the ethics code of the International Council of Museums urging the “inherent dignity” of human remains be respected.Glasgow’s nearby Hunterian Museum has decided to cover the more than 2,500-year-old body of Lady Shep-En-Hor in a specially designed textile while leaving her sarcophagus on view, the BBC reported.Egypt, also famed for its Nile cruises and Mediterranean and Red Sea beach resorts, targets attracting a record 20 million tourists this year and 22 million in 2027.More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: France protest: 575,000 people take part in demonstrations across major cities; 70,000 police deployed | What we know
item.description: Protests swept across France on Thursday, with an estimated 575,000 people taking to the streets in the biggest demonstrations since unrest began in September. While most rallies remained peaceful, clashes with police in Paris and Lyon led to arrests and injuries.
item.dc:creator: Swati Gandhi
item.content:encoded: Nationwide demonstrations continued across France on Thursday (local time), drawing roughly 575,000 protesters, according to government estimates, in the largest turnout recorded since the protests began in September.The protests were largely peaceful, despite some clashes with police in major cities like Paris and Lyon, as some public sector workers staged a one-day strike in a renewed challenge to President Emmanuel Macron, Reuters reported.While the Interior Ministry said 575,000 people attended the protests, the CGT union, one of the organisers, put the figure at 1.6 million.Nationwide demonstrations continue: Here's what we knowAccording to CNN, the demonstrations have expanded beyond students demanding better conditions in schools, drawing participation from trade unions and Yellow Vest protesters. The protests have also disrupted operations at schools, universities, railways and, to a lesser extent, hospitals.Several high-profile politicians also joined the protests, including presidential candidates Jean-Luc Mélenchon and Raphaël Glucksmann. The demonstrations follow protests over the high cost of living, public services and education, which have triggered the worst civil unrest in France in years.The unrest in France comes just months before a presidential election, which Macron cannot contest, putting added pressure on Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. He is preparing to meet workers' and employers' groups on November 9 (local time) to discuss concerns over the cost of living and salaries. The election could pit far-right candidate Marine Le Pen against hard-left rival Mélenchon in a second-round run-off.The strike also led to a drop in France's nuclear power output early on Thursday, while the Education Ministry said just over 15% of the country's teaching staff had joined the walkout.Largely peaceful protests in France turn violent: What we knowProtests got underway in Lyon and other cities, including Marseille and Nantes, during the morning, while the main march in Paris began later in the afternoon from Place de la République.At the start, the mood in Paris was festive, with a large group of participants singing "La Marseillaise" and some carnival-like floats. The one-day strike drew participants from energy workers and teachers, and the Eiffel Tower was shut down. However, there were no major disruptions to transport services in Paris.Two hours later, several people at the front of the march clashed with police, who fired tear gas. Citing Paris police, Reuters reported that several hooded individuals had committed acts of vandalism, prompting officers to intervene to stop the incidents and isolate those involved.In Lyon, southeastern France, about 470 km southeast of Paris, riot police used tear gas against protesters and charged at a group, some of whom shouted anti-police slogans. The Interior Ministry said police in Lyon were confronted by several hundred protesters. Although violence was contained, tensions remained high.As the demonstrations drew to a close, some protesters clashed with police, while authorities had to put out at least one small fire near the protest site. The Interior Ministry announced that at least 53 police officers had been injured and more than 448 people arrested.Around 70,000 police personnel were deployed across the country, a figure comparable to that of recent weekends. The French government defended police actions while maintaining that any instances of misconduct would be investigated.Ever since demonstrations turned violent roughly three weeks ago, authorities and shopkeepers have braced for similar scenes at each of the nationwide protests that followed.However, CNN reported that some train services were disrupted due to the demonstrations and striking workers. Citing the country's Health Ministry, it said that roughly 5% of hospital staff had participated in the strike, adding that "no significant disruption to healthcare services has been reported".The demonstrations highlight the growing discontent over living costs, public services and education, adding to the political pressure on Macron's government ahead of the next presidential election.(with agency inputs)

item.title: Petrol and diesel prices today, November 6: Check fuel cost in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru
item.description: West Texas Intermediate rose to trade near $91 a barrel on Friday, extending a rebound from a sharp selloff following a Democratic sweep of the US midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Livemint
item.content:encoded: Petrol and diesel prices today, November 6: Petrol and diesel prices remained largely steady across major cities today, even with the Centre eliminating the additional excise duty applicable to petrol exports.The cost of fuel varies across states and cities due to local taxes (Value Added Tax or VAT), freight charges, and other localised factors.Here is a look at the petrol and diesel prices in major metropolitan cities as of November 6:New Delhi: Petrol is retailing at ₹102.12 per litre, while diesel is priced at ₹95.20 per litre. The national capital continues to have relatively lower fuel prices compared to other metros.Mumbai: In the financial capital, petrol is priced at ₹111.21 per litre, and diesel costs ₹97.83 per litre.Chennai: Residents in Chennai are paying ₹107.76 per litre for petrol and ₹99.55 per litre for diesel.Kolkata: Petrol costs ₹113.51 per litre, while diesel costs ₹99.82 per litre.Bengaluru: Petrol is priced at ₹111.68 per litre, and diesel at ₹99.56 per litre.Hyderabad: Petrol costs ₹116.15 per litre, while diesel costs ₹104.23 per litre.Petrol and diesel prices in other metro cities today Source: GoodReturnsOil set for biggest weekly loss since April Oil was on track for the biggest weekly loss since April after a volatile stretch of trading, as investors weighed prospects for an end to the months-long war in the Middle East. West Texas Intermediate rose to trade near $91 a barrel on Friday, extending a rebound from a sharp selloff following a Democratic sweep of the US midterm elections. Still, prices are down more than 12% this week. While there are hopes for a faster end to the nine-month conflict, major differences remain. Tehran wants a US naval blockade of its ports lifted, sanctions eased, and frozen assets released before fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Still, the New York Times reported Iran is reviewing proposals about its nuclear program presented by mediators, suggesting recent diplomatic efforts by Qatar to prevent a resumption of full military conflict are having some success. Global benchmark Brent hit a six-month high in October as US President Donald Trump threatened renewed strikes on Iran following the midterms. For now, he is showing restraint, while Democratic control of both houses of Congress may constrain the administration’s ability to conduct further military action, Bloomberg reported.Trump met with his national security advisers to discuss Iran on Thursday as part of his weekly intelligence meeting, Axios reported, citing two unnamed US officials. He is considering three options: new strikes, continuing efforts to hobble Tehran economically, or cutting a deal that includes significant concessions to the Iranians, the report said.Despite frequent attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, there has been a revival in crude exports from the Persian Gulf. That has prompted Saudi Arabia to cut prices for buyers in Asia from levels already at a six-year low, as producers compete for market share.

item.title: Trump blames Democrats for market losses after US midterm elections; says ‘we’ll be bigger, stronger than ever before’
item.description: US President Donald Trump blamed Democrats for losses in Americans' 401(k) retirement portfolios following their sweeping midterm election victories. His remarks came amid a deepening selloff in artificial intelligence and technology stocks, raising concerns over market volatility.
item.dc:creator: Swati Gandhi
item.content:encoded: Days after Democrats secured sweeping victories in the US midterm elections, dealing major setbacks to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, Trump on Thursday (local time) blamed Democrats for losses in Americans' 401(k) portfolios amid a deepening selloff in artificial intelligence (AI) and technology-related stocks.Trump blames Democrats for market losses: Here's what he saidIn a social media post, Trump blamed Democrats for the market downturn, writing, "The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election. Such a sad thing to watch! It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this. Your 401(k)s have, therefore, dropped. Remember, it wasn’t Republicans; it was Dumocrats. Do not fear; however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!"In another post, the US president wrote, "The stock market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame." Equity markets extend losses on concerns over tighter AI regulationsTrump's remarks came as equity markets extended their losses on Thursday (local time) amid concerns that Democrats, who secured a sweeping victory in the midterm elections by gaining control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, could impose tighter regulations on the artificial intelligence industry, including the construction of data centres. Major chipmakers and other technology companies were among the worst-hit stocks, Bloomberg reported.In its worst trading session since March 2020, the Nasdaq 100 declined 6.4%, wiping out $2.3 trillion in market value. Treasuries rally as investors seek safer assets amid tech selloffUS government bonds rallied on Thursday as investors sought safer assets following a sharp selloff in major American technology stocks triggered by the Democrats' sweeping election victory.Yields on Treasury securities fell by as much as 12 basis points across different maturities, reaching their lowest levels since early September. Trading activity also picked up, with Treasury futures volumes running about 40% above their 20-day average. The flight to safer investments coincided with a 6.4% decline in the Nasdaq 100 and a 12% drop in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index.The bond market had also recorded its strongest monthly performance in more than two years in October, as concerns grew over the long-term sustainability of heavy investments in AI infrastructure. Investors increasingly shifted funds out of equities and into government debt amid questions over whether the scale of AI-related capital expenditure could be sustained.Trump's support for AI and stock market gainsDespite widespread opposition to data centre expansion, Trump has strongly backed the industry and favoured a light-touch regulatory approach. At the same time, he has repeatedly touted stock market gains, fuelled partly by investor enthusiasm for AI, as a measure of economic success in his speeches and social media posts.Trump's response to Republican losses in the midterm electionsAfter weeks of questioning the election's legitimacy in the event of Republican losses, Trump said on Tuesday night that he would accept the midterm results. However, he deflected responsibility for the party's poor performance, claiming he would have won by a landslide had his name been on the ballot, while acknowledging that Democrats had done a "good job".On Wednesday, Trump blamed high fuel prices, which had risen amid the US war in Iran, for the Republican Party's midterm losses, while continuing to defend the conflict as justified.(with Bloomberg inputs)

item.title: Wisconsin Baby Dies of Measles in First State Death in 36 Years
item.description: Wisconsin reported its first measles death in more than three decades on Thursday, the latest state to suffer a fatality from a virus that was long eradicated in the US but recently surged back amid a wave of anti-vaccine sentiment.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- Wisconsin reported its first measles death in more than three decades on Thursday, the latest state to suffer a fatality from a virus that was long eradicated in the US but recently surged back amid a wave of anti-vaccine sentiment.The death occurred in an infant, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services said in a statement. It is the third US measles death within the last week — matching the number of deaths in all of 2025. In the preceding 25 years, the US typically had no deaths.Across the US, measles has been spreading at an increasing rate as vaccination uptake has declined. That’s eroded the herd immunity that protects people who cannot be vaccinated like infants and the immunocompromised. At least 45 states have reported infections for a total of 4,852 people, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The highly contagious virus has been spreading in the southwestern part of Wisconsin and nine people have been hospitalized in connection with the outbreak, according to the health department.“Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease,” Wisconsin State Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement. With the US measles case count at its highest in decades, its long-held status as a measles eliminated country is under threat. An outside group of experts is scheduled to meet next week and review the data to determine whether the US has seen continued transmission of the disease for more than 12 months. This week, Pennsylvania confirmed a sixth death from measles and New York reported its first. Utah, South Carolina and Texas have also seen particularly bad flareups of measles over the last year.Wisconsin said local healthcare providers and public health staff have delivered more than 42,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine since August. No vaccine is perfect, but the MMR is 97% effective after two doses. One to three people out of 1,000 are likely to die from measles, according to the CDC. The respiratory infection can cause flu-like symptoms and a distinct red rash across the body. Complications include brain swelling, pneumonia and death. The CDC has confirmed only four of the deaths this year. After Pennsylvania reported its first fatalities, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested the state’s governor Josh Shapiro may have fabricated them for political gain — sparking a verbal dispute. The CDC is working on a national measles death definition with an outside group of epidemiologists.More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.
